newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia forgives, not forgets, Singapore's Lee.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia forgives, not forgets, Singapore's Lee.

text.p: Malaysia may forgive Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew for saying unkind things about a Malaysian state but they will not soon forget it, analysts said on Wednesday.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi told reporters after a cabinet meeting on Wednesday the government accepted Lee's apology but the episode had deeply hurt all Malaysians. "Restoration of the old level of relationship would take time," he added.
Analysts said Malaysia would look for signs that Singapore was dealing with what Kuala Lumpur sees as the root cause of the periodically strained ties -- Singapore's superiority complex.

"Malaysians think Singapore looks down on them," said Bruce Gale, regional manager of Political & Economic Risk Consultancy Ltd. "Lee's remark essentially said you're inferior to us and that just inflames them."
Lee said in a statement on Monday he would ask a local court to delete a remark in an affidavit saying the Malaysian state of Johor "was notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".

That move followed a rare public apology last week by the 73-year-old Lee, who led the fight for Singapore's independence and was its prime minister from 1959 until 1990. He now has an elder statesman's role as senior minister.

"Technically it's over, but the memory will linger," said Mohamed Jabbar Hassan of the Institute for Strategic and International Studies. "There has to be some serious soul searching in Singapore about how it deals with its friends and close neighbours."

Author and political columnist Rustan Sani saw Lee's remarks as part of a pattern. "It's a question of whether this has put an end to the pattern or put an end to this particular incident...I think it will flare up again.
"Over the years, there has developed an attitude that Malaysians are more racial than Singapore, less meritocratic than Singapore, less efficient, less clean.

"That has always been in the back of not only Lee's mind but many other people in Singapore as well. So, whenever we have an incident of this sort, it comes to the foreground what has been in the background."

Last year, Lee hit a raw nerve across the causeway over the Johor Strait separating the two countries when he said some day Singapore might be forced to re-unite with Malaysia if the island state was unable to compete on its own.
But he added Singapore would only do so if Malaysia adopted meritocratic policies.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad accused Lee of conjuring up Malaysia as a "bogeyman" to scare voters ahead of polls that were eventually held in January.

The reference to meritocracy re-opened an old wound. The predominantly Chinese city state of Singapore and Malaysia were united in the Malaysia Federation from 1963 to 1965 before Singapore was expelled for opposing state policies favouring special rights for ethnic Malays.
Lee led a campaign for meritocracy, saying Singaporeans could be reduced to "second-class citizens" in Malaysia.
Then a fiery member of parliament, Mahathir crossed swords with Lee in the legislature over the issue and the two since have never been the best of friends.

Malaysians are still not altogether happy with Lee's apology and move to withdraw the offending remarks from his court affadavit, both of which were done by issuing statements. Lee, himself, has not personally commented about the incident."
Lee's controversial remarks were part of an affidavit he made in court on January 27 in his libel suit against opposition politician Tang Liang Hong.

Tang fled to Johor Baru, capital of Johor state, immediately after losing a race for parliament in Singapore's general elections on January 2, saying he had received death threats in Singapore. Lee questioned why he would feel safer in Johor.

Lee issued his apology a day after an extraordinary protest in Johor, in which demonstrators from the youth wing of Mahathir's United Malays National Organisation brandished signs calling Lee "stupid", "senile" and "a bloody idiot". Mahathir was seen greeting the demonstrators with a wide grin.
